pages.x: Armenians had lived in eastern Anatolia since ancient times, and their kingdom was the first to make Christianity its religion, by tradition in the year 301. By 1914 some two million lived in the Ottoman Empire, many of them farmers, traders and craftsmen. Massacres in the 1890s had already killed a hundred thousand or more.

After a heavy defeat by Russia in the Caucasus, the Young Turk government led by Talaat, Enver and Djemal branded the Armenians traitors. On the night of 24 April 1915 police in Constantinople rounded up hundreds of Armenian writers, priests and leaders, and most of them were later killed. Armenians remember the date every year.

In the months that followed, Armenian men were shot, and women, children and the old were marched over mountains into the Syrian desert toward Deir ez-Zor, with little food or water. Hundreds of thousands died of killing, hunger, thirst and disease. Others were forced to convert, and children were taken into Muslim homes.

Many saw it. The American ambassador, Henry Morgenthau, cabled Washington that a campaign of race extermination was under way, and a German army medic, Armin Wegner, secretly photographed the camps. Some Turks and Kurds hid Armenians at the risk of their own lives, and a few officials refused to carry out the orders.

A Polish Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, had followed the killing of the Armenians as a student. In 1944 he made up a new word, genocide, for the deliberate destruction of a people, pointing to the Armenians and to the Nazi murder of the Jews. In 1948 the United Nations made genocide a crime under international law.

Armenian life in Anatolia, thousands of years old, was almost wiped out, and the survivors scattered from Beirut to Los Angeles. Most historians and many countries call it genocide. Turkey accepts that many Armenians died but rejects the word, and the question still divides the two nations.
